data.title: Inflation Slides in France, Spain on Declining Fuel Prices — 3rd Update
data.description:
By Ed Frankl and Paul Hannon

The annual rate of inflation in France and Spain fell more sharply than expected in November as fuel prices declined, while the eurozone economy grew less rapidly than previously estimated in the three months through September.

Investors expect the European Central Bank to raise its key interest rate next month for a third time since the start of the war between the U.S. and Iran. But the central bank has said it will be "data-dependent" in its policy decisions, and the latest readings from the eurozone economy point to weaker inflationary pressures.

Consumer prices in the eurozone's second-largest economy were 3.2% higher than in the same month of 2025, a lower annual rate of inflation than the 3.7% recorded in October, France's statistics office said Friday. Economists polled last week by The Wall Street Journal expected a 3.6% rate of inflation.

In Spain, figures also published Friday showed the annual rate of inflation also dropped sharply in November, to 4.1% from 4.9% in October.

Oil prices have fallen since the outcome of U.S. midterm elections fueled hopes of a lasting resolution to the conflict, although they remain above prewar levels. As a result, prices of gasoline and other fuels have declined.

However, European natural gas prices remain near multiyear highs, which will keep household energy prices elevated throughout the colder winter months.

The ECB has raised its key rate twice so far this year, judging that the surge in energy prices was too great to ignore. Investors are primed for another hike before the end of the year.

The EU said last week that it expects French inflation to peak at 4.3% in the first quarter of 2027 due to further increases in energy prices and how they pass through into food and services.

Yet incoming data shows few signs of those energy costs spilling over into other parts of the economy. Services inflation in France fell in November due to a sharp decrease in prices for accommodation and transport services.

Revised figures for economic growth in the three months through September indicate that the eurozone economy has been less resilient in the face of higher energy prices than previously estimated.

The French statistics agency on Friday said the country's gross domestic product sank 0.2% in the third quarter, having previously estimated the drop at 0.1%. Earlier this week, Germany's statistics agency cut its estimate for third-quarter growth.

"A weakening labor market and growing fears of unemployment will keep households cautious. At the same time, weak demand and a lack of visibility will continue to weigh on business investment. The outlook for 2027 remains very gloomy," Charlotte de Montpellier, an economist at ING, wrote in a note to clients.

French consumer spending was flat in October, data also published Friday showed. While surveys of purchasing managers for November showed steady economic growth in Germany, there was a deepening downturn in activity in France.

Amid those signs of weakening inflationary pressures, the ECB's own survey of 19,000 consumers between Oct. 1 and Nov. 2 yielded some concerning news for policymakers. It found that households expected prices to rise by 3.5% over the coming 12 months, up from 3.1% in September.

However, expectations may fall back in response to November's inflation figures, although the next survey won't be released until early next year and the ECB announces its policy decision on Dec. 17.

data.title: He Lost His Wife-Then Devised an Estate-Planning Fix Anyone Can Do — WSJ
data.description:
By Ashlea Ebeling | Design and Illustrations by Annie Ng

The Economics of Growing Old

This story is part of a WSJ series on aging. A new piece will publish each day through Dec. 1.

Like many couples, Tim and Christine Corrigan had their lanes.

He was an assurance partner at PwC, and she was a lawyer-turned-writer and homemaker. He handled the big-ticket financial tasks, like making annual mega-backdoor 401(k) Roth conversions, while she managed bills for the family of five — everything from garbage collection to car insurance.

After Christine died unexpectedly while awaiting surgery at age 58, grief quickly gave way to time-consuming work. He did a "reverse audit" of the family's vendors, transferred a boatload of financial accounts and went down the rabbit hole of all those things in life that are subscription-based, he said.

He'd finish one thing, and something else would pop up. So he decided to write it all down in a Word document.

He calls it the playbook — a 30-page distillation of a life lived together, and the one he is carrying on without her. It's an instruction manual of sorts for his three children, so they won't have to go on the same domestic expedition one day. He keeps it in his home office in Southport, N.C. Writing an opening cover letter addressed to his children, now 21, 25 and 30, brought him to tears.

"Kids," the letter begins, "I am sorry you are having to consult this book. Mom and I loved you each so very much."

Aging gracefully increasingly means packaging up your life so that next of kin can make sense of it all. It's a contrast with earlier generations who tended to avoid talking about estate planning. Corrigan, 60, was the executor for both of his parents' estates, and they left no instructions.

Preparing an organizer and sharing it with the people who will need it is an often-neglected but essential step after signing a will or trust. Fail to do so and you send your heirs on a scavenger hunt at the most stressful time of their lives.

Corrigan's playbook is a do-it-yourself version of popular commercially available "death box" organizers where people list financial accounts, contacts and more. A Nokbox, or next-of-kin box, is a plastic container with color-coded folders and worksheets. Buried In Work's CLEAR Kit is a system of worksheets and guidance in binders, with an online version that recently launched. Family Folder, launched last year, lets families upload and share key documents.

"Ideally, you want to be sharing this information before death or even before someone becomes ill," said Tony Staunton, who founded Family Folder after his mother was diagnosed with Alzheimer's, to help him, his dad and siblings handle the load of her care.

Corrigan's playbook addresses major pain points he encountered as he navigated the loss of his wife. He didn't know what bills got paid via check, credit card or bill pay, and at what frequency.

One night a son called him from the road and said his car insurance was expiring the next day. "I ask, 'Well, did you pay it?' To which I got back, 'Mom always did.' I had no idea," Corrigan said.

He stared at her phone and took stabs at the password. It turned out the kids knew it.

Once he got in, he kept his wife's phone active. Two months after her death, a text came through that a pressure-washer operator was coming at 9 a.m. to clean pollen off the house.

The playbook lists all his vendors and what gets paid monthly, quarterly, semiannually or annually. It has usernames, email addresses and passwords for his iPhone, three iPads, desktop PC and laptop PC.

The playbook lists who to contact in the first 72 hours: A friend who is a Roman Catholic priest, his attorney, his church, the funeral home, PwC partner affairs. Then it provides context, that the executor gets a stipend, how his life-insurance policy works, that PwC prepares his tax returns and estimated tax payments, and how a retired Coast Guard captain friend should be the go-to person for anything to do with his 27-foot power boat.

After he got an NC Quick Pass "balance low" reminder on Christine's email, he turned in her pass and added a section to the playbook with the tag numbers for his two BMWs.

The book goes beyond the mundane. After struggling with writing her obituary, he wrote an outline of his for his children, "so they have a place to start."

The playbook explains what to do if there is still money in his $300,000 health savings account: Look in a hanging folder labeled HSA for unreimbursed receipts to submit. His death shouldn't put a stop to tax savings.

His thinking: It helps to err on the side of putting it all in there.

Talking to heirs about where the death box or playbook is, and what is in it, is just as important as gathering the information. "If you organize all your information and nobody knows how to find it, it's like you did nothing," said Adam Zuckerman, founder of Buried In Work.

Three months after Christine's death, Corrigan took his playbook version 1.0 on the family vacation she had planned to the Florida Keys. He shared it with his children, along with a high-level balance sheet.

"They really didn't want to talk about it to tell you the truth, but we were all together," he said.

Coral Mitchell, a 64-year-old retired director of accounting in Wilton, Conn., said she would have been lost after her dad's death in 2019 if he hadn't created a death book. He shared where to find it and discussed how he was counting on her to help care for her mother after he died.

When an insurance company claimed his pension terminated at his death, Mitchell had the paperwork to refute it. Her mother got payments for almost five more years until her death. The book had instructions to give the 20-gauge shotgun in the attic to the local police. It included a map showing the septic-tank location, so she had it on hand when the technician arrived to pump it out. "I wouldn't have known," she said.

Mitchell, in turn, created her own death book. She's told her best friend, whom she's named executor of her estate, where it is and what is in it. "I'm pretty open about death," she said.

For Corrigan, the playbook made him realize he could simplify his own life. He consolidated assets under a new financial adviser. He accelerated distributions from an inherited IRA from his mother. And he is talking to his attorney and financial adviser about starting a lifetime gifting plan to keep his estate under the federal estate-tax threshold.

The Corrigans moved to North Carolina in August 2023 and were still in the process of updating their wills when Christine died in early 2025. Having a New Jersey will added complexity and legal fees to the probate process. Corrigan is working with a new attorney on North Carolina estate-planning documents and is planning to give her a copy of the playbook to keep in her firm's vault, along with his will.

Back from a two-week trip to Spain last month, Corrigan set about updating the playbook to include the contact information for his new attorney, along with information about a charitable fund he established to grant trade-school scholarships through the St. James Service Club, where Christine volunteered.

"Old contacts are as good as no contacts," he said. "You have to be diligent about keeping it up-to-date."

The playbook, born out of grief, remains a living document.

data.title: 2026 in photos: AI, robots and new technology
data.description:
Technology advanced rapidly this year and long-anticipated developments in artificial intelligence, drones and robots appeared to be materializing, fast.

AI now permeates almost every aspect of life, from fashion and food to counseling and education, for good and for bad. In schools, for instance, teachers are having to rethink how they teach and test in a world of smart chatbots available to all. But AI-enabled technology can also allow medical students to train with virtual simulations, or help children who are hard of hearing understand science lessons.

Illustrating technology through photography is not always easy. While robots certainly can be eye-catching — particularly when paired with humans in unexpected ways — concepts like AI or cybercrime often need a creative touch.

Sometimes that might be through a glimpse into the world of the billionaire executives who run the big tech firms. Or it might be by documenting the backlash to the water-thirsty data centers springing up to power the AI boom, or by photographing in the bunkers of Ukraine where drones are transforming warfare.

And sometimes, it just means taking really cool robot pictures.

data.title: Deutsche Asset Mgmt: US Stocks Highly Reliant on AI; Short-term Jitters Expected to Persist
data.description:
Vincenzo Vedda, Chief Investment Officer, Deutsche Asset Management, expressing market views, said nervousness in the US stock market continues to intensify, with tech stocks coming under gross pressure. The market may reassess the risk-reward profile of the AI sector over the coming months, while investors are increasingly focused on when massive AI investments will generate broader economic returns. Companies' reliance on external financing is also facing stricter scrutiny.

The firm said bond issuance to support AI investments has leapfrogged recently, leading to a steep rise in risk premiums for tech corporate bonds. data.title: Premiums inch up but capped by inventory recovery at key hubs
data.description:
Spot fuel oil premiums edged up on Friday, though signs of recovering inventories at key trading hubs in recent weeks capped market strength while incoming supplies into Singapore remained ample to meet demand, market sources said.

Timespreads for both very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) and high sulphur fuel oil (HSFO) markets widened in backwardation for prompt months on Friday, data from sources showed, lifting spot premiums day on day despite broadly thin trade.

For the near term, supply replenishment appeared ample at key trading hubs including Singapore, Fujairah and Rotterdam, which have seen steady to rising onshore inventories.

Meanwhile, fuel oil cracks traded higher from the previous close for December contracts. The 380-cst HSFO crack (FO380BRTCKMc1) climbed day on day to a discount of $3.20 a barrel on Friday, while the VLSFO crack (LFO05SGBRTCMc1) rose slightly to a premium of $18.85 a barrel.

Amid the recent weakness in gasoline markets, some blendstocks are expected to divert to the VLSFO blending pool instead, some sources said.

INVENTORY DATA

- Fuel oil inventories in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp hub (STK-FO-ARA) eased 4.3% week on week though continued to hold above 1 million tons in the week to November 26, Dutch consultancy Insights Global data showed.

OTHER NEWS

- Oil prices rose on Friday as ongoing attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy infrastructure heightened concerns over oil supply from the conflict-hit Middle East.

- OPEC+ is likely to maintain its oil output targets for at least the first quarter of 2027 at a meeting on Sunday, two people with knowledge of the talks said, as the Iran war continues to disrupt Middle East exports and disagreements persist over some nations' oil production capacity assessments.

- Asian gasoline margins flipped into negative territory on Thursday amid expectations of higher supplies and lower demand, while a rally in crude oil benchmarks also pressured the crack, traders and analysts said.

- Indonesia's government is considering raising subsidised fuel prices in early 2027 for the first time in five years, four people familiar with the matter said, as high global oil prices and a weak rupiah increase pressure on the G20 economy's finances.

data.title: Dubai's Benchmark Stock Index Erases Wartime Losses as Banks, Property Shares Rise
data.description:
By Farhan Rafid

DOHA, Qatar--Dubai stocks rose on Friday, erasing losses since the Iran war began in late February and putting the emirate's benchmark among the Gulf's best-performing equity indexes this year.

The Dubai Financial Market General Index rose 1.2% to 6,563.30 points, surpassing its closing level of 6,503.50 points on Feb. 27, the last trading session before the war began. The index has gained nearly 14% so far this month.

Index heavyweight Emaar Properties rose 2%, while Dubai Islamic Bank and Emirates NBD gained 3% and 2.2%, respectively. Shares of exchange operator Dubai Financial Market jumped 7.1%.

The market's recovery comes despite continued disruptions to regional trade and travel. Dubai's government introduced economic incentives worth 2.5 billion dirhams ($681 million) across two packages earlier this year, including fee exemptions and payment deferrals for businesses.

Dubai's real gross domestic product contracted 2.3% in the first half from a year earlier, though financial and insurance activities expanded 8.8%, according to data released in October by the Dubai Data and Statistics Establishment.

Dubai was the only major Gulf equity market to have recorded gains this year as of last week, according to a report by SICO, a Bahrain-based investment bank.

Dubai's benchmark was also up 3.3% for the year, compared with a 1.2% decline in the S&P GCC Index.

The Dubai market's resilience has been driven by a handful of stocks rather than a broad-based rally, SICO analysts said. A sharp recovery remains dependent on a resolution to the regional conflict given the emirate's reliance on tourism and population inflows, they said.

The analysts remain positive on Dubai's commercial real-estate sector but see a risk of oversupply in the residential segment. Banks' asset quality remains closely tied to property prices, though lending in neighboring Abu Dhabi could help support loan growth, they said.

The total value of securities traded on Dubai's exchange rose 22% from a year earlier to 162 billion dirhams in the first nine months, according to a report by Kamco Invest, a Kuwait-based investment firm.
